notes: Faster with big bibles: opening a library no longer compares every bible entry with every other (with 600 entries that took over a second each time), and the note about entries filed under the wrong kind is worked out in a moment instead of a fifth of a second after every change.
Where each entry appears in the books is kept between sessions, so the bible and Planning open straight away after the first time instead of reading every chapter again.
The corkboard is several times quicker to draw: its cork is drawn from one tile, and only the cards on screen are drawn.
The stars in the top bar twinkle more gently and rest while another window is in front, so the Studio uses next to nothing while it waits.

Review, Typesetting, Preview and Publishing have no sidebars and no details panel, so every workspace now has the same layout: a header with the book, its parts as tabs, one tools menu, and details in a card at the right when there's something to show.

Review: Changes, Snapshots, Names, Comments and Goals are tabs, and Review tools ▾ has Make a review copy… and Import a reader's comments…. A snapshot you click, and your daily goal on the Goals tab, show in a card beside the page.

Typesetting: a bar over the pages has Export PDF…, Design (the design's choices in a card beside the pages; click it to put them away for more room), Contents ▾ (each chapter with its page number) and Typeset tools ▾ (the page size, the text width, any notes about the setting, and Publishing).

Preview: a bar over the device has Back and Next, Reader's settings (the device, the page colour, text size and font in a card beside it), Contents ▾ for the chapters, and Preview tools ▾ with Refresh from the text.

Publishing: the editions are tabs along the top, the chosen edition's name, ISBN, kind, trim and design are in a card at the right, and Publishing tools ▾ has Add an edition…, the cover designer, the print design, reading it as an ebook and the book's page.
Settings › Appearance has Chapter details in Writing in place of the details panel, and F3 and F4 are now Writing's outline and chapter details.
Writing has more room for the text: the outline is narrower (F3 still hides it), and the details panel is gone until you want it.

A bar over the page shows the chapter you're in: its kind, its name (click it to rename it there; Enter keeps it and goes on to the text, Esc puts it back), its status (click it to change it) and its words.

At the bar's right, Details (or F4) opens the chapter's details in a card beside the text, and Chapter tools ▾ has Details, Earlier versions…, Plan it on the corkboard, New chapter, New scene, New part, Move up, Move down, Import into this book… and Move to Trash.
A picture or a comment chosen in the text opens its details in the same card. The top bar's details button in Writing shows and hides the chapter's details.

The Library has no sidebar. Your worlds, All books, Independent books, Artwork and the Trash are tabs along the top, with Library tools ▾ at the end of the row (a new world, book or series, importing a book, opening a world from GitHub, backing up, exporting, another library). A world's or series' details sit in a card at the right of its page.

Clicking a book opens its own page: its cover and series line, its words against the target, its chapters and status, and the ways in (Open in Writing, or Continue writing at the chapter you were on; Plan; The bible; Book tools ▾).

A book's page has tabs. Overview has the synopsis (click it to change it, where it's shown) and the manuscript. Book settings has what the details panel held, in cards: title, subtitle, status, format and tags; author, pen name, genre, language, edition, ISBN and trim; the cover; and the series it's in. Editions lists each edition with its ISBN. Import & export gathers bringing a manuscript or a plan in, and sending the book out as print-ready PDF and EPUB, a proof, a review copy or the plan as text. History has when it last changed and its snapshots, with Take a snapshot.

Planning has no sidebar either. Its header shows the book with its progress (click it to set the target), + Chapter and Plan tools ▾ (the target, a new thread, importing and exporting the plan, Writing and the bible). Corkboard, Timeline, Structure and the new Threads are tabs, with All statuses ▾, Any viewpoint ▾ and Any thread ▾ at the end of the row.
On the corkboard, a card's details open beside it as a pop-over; the cross or Esc puts them away. On the other views they're a card at the right of the page.
Threads shows each plot thread as a card, with how many cards it runs through; click one to name it, colour it and say what it's about.

A warmer look: the Studio's pages are warm paper, with cards that sit up from it on soft shadows, and gold labels over the page titles. The night-sky bar and the workspaces down the left stay as they were.

Worldbuilding has no sidebar and no details panel. The top of the bible shows the world's name, + New entry and Bible tools ▾, a menu with the Glossary, Languages, Relationships, Fonts, Checks, image boards, Share the bible, Sync with GitHub, the world's books, importing pages and Reset the bible.

The kinds of entry are tabs along the top of the bible, with how many each has (kinds with nothing in them yet are under More), and the find box sits at the end of the tab row. Under the tabs, a kind's entries can be narrowed by gender, race, realm or type with a click on a chip, and characters can be grouped by gender, sexuality or race from a small menu.

Entries are edited where they're shown. Click the name, the summary, the details, a section, a book's notes or the notes and type there; Enter (Ctrl+Enter in longer text) or a click elsewhere keeps it, and Esc puts back what was there. A section with choices shows them as buttons while it's being written.

On an entry's page, Add a section ▾ lists the sections still to write, the books it has no notes for yet, and changing the sections every page of its kind has. The ⋯ button holds the rest: its kind, gender, race and the like, other names, how it's said, the picture, spoilers, filling the page from what you've copied, and Move to Trash. The kind and the gender or race over the name can be clicked to change them too.
A new entry opens with its name ready to type. An entry with no picture has a place for one: click it to choose a picture, or drag one from its gallery onto it.

Pages of the bible's tools (Languages, Relationships, Fonts, Share, Sync, image boards, family trees, the map, the Glossary and Checks) have ‹ The bible and Bible tools ▾ along the top, and those with details show them in a card at the right of the page.

Sync with GitHub works for big worlds: GitHub gave up (“your request timed out”) when a whole world was sent as one piece, so it now goes in batches, and a batch GitHub can't take is sent again in smaller ones.

While it sends, the Sync page counts the files (“Sending to GitHub: 62 of 129 files…”), and once the repository has been checked the note says the world is being sent instead of staying on “Checking the repository…”.
Settings › About has Visit the website, which opens Writing Studio's page on NorthRay Software's website in your browser.

Every drop-down in the Studio looks the same: a box like a text field, the choice on the left and a small arrow on the right (Review's chapter and version choosers, Typesetting's trim size and typeface, Share the bible, a series' book kind).
Text fields have the same rounded corners as the buttons.
Typesetting's bar no longer overlaps: where you are sits between the view switch and the guides and zoom, and drops the “(1 of 7)” when there isn't room.
Typesetting lists its designs by name; only the chosen one shows its description (point at the others to read theirs).
Review, Preview and Publishing explain themselves in one line in the panel instead of several paragraphs.

Every place on the rail opens something: Planning, Review, Typesetting, Preview and Publishing open the book you're looking at, a series' first book, or the book you last wrote in, instead of asking you to choose one first.
On a series page, Reading order / Chronological and Bookshelf / List no longer overlap; when a row of controls is full, the view switch moves to the next line (All books and world pages too).
The Library's search box matches the bible's: a magnifier, and the same rounded corners as the buttons.
The Trash is a quiet list: Restore shows on the row you point at, and an empty Trash is one line.
A new library's page is one line and one button, with Import, New world and Open a world from GitHub in the usual row.
Planning's panel notes and the timeline's introduction are one line each; the timeline's + button shows one plus.
The ‹ Library link is gone from every workspace's sidebar (the rail has it).
Icons with curves (Undo, Sync, Person, Share) are drawn the same way on every PC.
Worldbuilding has the calm look too: no back link beside the rail, one plain line when entries may be filed under the wrong kind, and page introductions of one line.
On an entry's page, a section's Edit button shows when you point at that section (Tab still reaches it), so the page reads as writing.
The buttons for sections still to write look like every other button, and the one being written is outlined.
Removing a map, an image board, a language or notes kept for a book happens at once, with Undo in the note.
While an entry is open, the list you came from stays chosen in the sidebar; chosen and pointed-at rows look the same in every sidebar.
An empty kind or an empty list of languages says one thing and has one button (+ New character, + New language).

A rail down the left side holds the workspaces (Library, Write, Plan, World, Review, Typeset, Preview, Publish) with an icon and a word each, and Settings at its foot. Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+8 open them top to bottom; the bookshelf and list views of the Library moved to Ctrl+Shift+1 and Ctrl+Shift+2.

One search box in the top bar (Ctrl+K) finds chapters and scenes, bible entries (by their other names too), books, worlds, the workspaces and commands as you type. Up and Down choose, Enter opens, Esc leaves it.
Every button has one look: a soft frame that lifts when you point at it, with a small icon beside its words. Rows of buttons wrap onto another line when a page is narrow instead of running off it.
The chosen row in every left sidebar looks the same, and the outline's buttons are + Chapter, + Scene and + Part, side by side.
Moving a chapter, scene, book, series, world or picture to the Trash happens at once, with Undo in the note at the bottom right, instead of asking first.
Fewer notes: nothing pops up to say a book was moved or added to a series or board, since you can see it there. The details panel's hints are one short line.
An empty Writing page says one thing and has one button (+ Chapter).
NorthRay Capture is told everyone in a chapter's Who's there (not only six), for its Writing card's scrolling cast row.

Importing a plan replaces the book's plan instead of adding to it. Chapters are matched ignoring numbers and symbols ("Steel and Snow" finds "1. 🗡 Steel and Snow", "Chapter 13" finds "13. Chapter 13"), take the plan's synopsis, viewpoint, place, who's there, time, threads and beats, and are put in its order; their titles and writing stay.

Empty parts, chapters and scenes the plan doesn't have go to the Trash; anything with writing is always kept, and named afterwards. Where an earlier import added every chapter twice, importing the plan again keeps the written copies and clears the empty ones.
Thread descriptions are replaced rather than repeated, and a thread's chapter numbers are only used when the outline doesn't give each chapter its threads.
Sexuality works like gender: characters can be grouped by it, list rows show it, and cards have a small banded mark beside the gender sign (point at it for the word).

Sync with GitHub (Worldbuilding): keep a world in a private GitHub repository of your own and write on more than one computer. Everything in the world goes: series, books with their chapters, plans and comments, the bible, boards, languages, fonts and pictures. The token is kept in Windows Credential Manager; there's no NorthRay account.
Open a world from GitHub (Library, Worlds) brings a synced world onto another computer, where it stays synced.

Syncing happens on its own: when the library opens, every few minutes while you're changing things, every ten minutes for the other computer's changes, and when Writing Studio closes. Sync now does it at once.

Changed on two computers before they synced: a chapter keeps the newer text and the other becomes a saved version in Review, Changes; bible entries keep the newer; links from both computers are kept. The Sync page lists what was changed on both.
Pictures are stored once under a name made from their contents, so each is uploaded once and another computer downloads only what it lacks. Writing Studio warns before using a public repository.

Sexuality: characters have a Sexuality choice beside Gender or sex (Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Heterosexual, Pansexual, Asexual, Aromantic, Queer, Questioning, Unknown, Not said, or your own words). Imported pages fill it from a "Sexuality:" or "Orientation:" line, and the sidebar groups characters by it.
From: a character's hometown or home realm is its own relationship, separate from where they live now. A page can say "From: Highcliff" and "Lives in: Valona"; the place lists them as Hometown of.

One Pictures area per entry: the gallery and the entry's boards are together. Drag a picture onto the main picture (at the top of the page or the tile marked Main) to swap them, or onto a board to add it there.
Each series counts its own books. In Notes per book, "Alvora Chronicles Book 2" or "Book 1 of the Envoy series" picks that series' book. "Book 2" alone works when only one series has a Book 2.

The exported bible holds more: notes for books still to come, Appears in (the chapters and scenes where the entry is in Who's there), each entry's boards, the main picture's caption, and a list of what's pinned on a map in the PDF.

Who's there: in Planning, each chapter and scene lists the characters and creatures present, chosen from the bible with the ones named in its text first. Someone only mentioned isn't counted, and a shared surname no longer brings in every Smith. The card shows them, outlines read and write a "Characters:" line, and Capture's cast list follows it (a chapter with no one chosen still goes by the names in its text).

Worldbuilding is quick with big bibles: only the cards on screen are drawn, and entries and their links are looked up directly. With 600 entries a frame took about 3.6 seconds and now takes about a tenth of a second (measured in Wine, which draws without the graphics card).

Cards or List: entries can be shown as one-line rows. With many families, Family trees shows the eight biggest and All for the rest; long sidebar lists of races or realms show the five with most entries and N more.
Creatures' families are in the bible: a creature's Family in the PDF and on the website, and their family trees with the characters'.
Writing Studio keeps a short list of the books you've written in lately, with the chapter you were on, for NorthRay Launcher's Jump back in.
NorthRay Launcher can open a book at its chapter, whether Writing Studio is closed or already open. If the book is in another library, Writing Studio says so instead.

Former partners: "Ex-husband", "Ex-wife", "Former partner" or "Divorced from" (or + Former partner on a page) keeps someone as the parent of their children without drawing them as a couple. Pages list them under Former partners; the tree marks them Ex-partner.

Engaged couples: "Fiancé", "Fiancée", "Betrothed" or "Engaged to" links two people as engaged. They're drawn as a couple, and the one with a gender is named as fiancé or fiancée. + Partner asks for partner, married, engaged or former partner, and clicking a partner changes which.

Triplets: "Triplets" (or Triplet under + Brother or sister) links all three, so linking one to the other two makes those two triplets as well. They stand together in the tree and come down from one point.
Creatures have a Family part: parents, partners, brothers and sisters (twins and triplets too) and children, all creatures, with their own family tree.
After importing pages, the note names any character with family but no gender, who would otherwise be called sibling, child or partner rather than sister, son or wife.

Founded and Founded by, Used and Used by, Mentor of, Scene of and Origin of are built in for the kinds they suit, so imports no longer make them your world's own relationships. A "Used by" you made before now counts as the built-in one.
Notes per book match titles with a colon in them, such as "Alvora: The Fall of Valona", so they no longer have to go by number.

Notes for a book that isn't in Writing Studio yet are kept on the entry under the title you gave (shown on its page, with Remove), and move onto the book when a book of that title or number is added. They no longer fall into Notes.
Each line under a book in Notes per book is a paragraph of its own, and a line starting like a sentence ("Later: …") stays with the book above it instead of being taken for another book.

Pictures in imports: a "Picture:" line takes a picture file's path for the entry's main picture, and lines under "Gallery:" add pictures to its gallery, each with a caption after a bar ("art/tom.png | Tom at the forge"). Paths can be whole or start from the imported file's folder; the pictures go into Artwork too.
Renaming through an import: a page is found by a name on its "Formerly:" line, or by one of its other names, and the entry is renamed instead of a second one being made.

Removing and merging through an import: "Remove: yes" puts a page's entry in the Trash; "Merge into: House Malrok" merges it into another entry; "Merged from: Sun Fire" on the page you keep does the same the other way round.

Import many pages says beforehand how many pages rename, merge or remove entries, and lists each one afterwards, with any pictures that couldn't be read. Ctrl+Z brings merged and removed entries back.
The blank page to fill in has Picture and Gallery lines.

Import planning fills in the chapters a book already has instead of adding them again: each part, chapter and scene is matched by its title (a "Chapter 3:" in front is ignored), or a chapter by its number among the story's chapters, and its synopsis, status, target, viewpoint, place, when, threads and beats are filled in from the plan. What the plan leaves out stays as it was; anything not matched is added.
"Chapter 3" and "Chapter 3: Ashes" lines start a chapter in a plan, as "Chapter:" does.
The note after importing says how many parts, chapters and scenes were filled in.

NorthRay Capture shows more of what you're writing: the chapter's status and target, its viewpoint character and place (with their pictures from the world bible), its story day, who's in it, any writing sprint, which part of the Studio you're in, and your world's colour.
Nothing is sent anywhere else: it's the same summary file on your PC that Capture already read.
Timeline: drag a card from below onto the timeline to place it, and zoom with Ctrl and the mouse wheel or the −, Fit and + buttons.
Lanes by viewpoint, plot thread or place, or one lane. Each chapter and scene can say where it happens (a place from the bible), in its panel or with “Place:” in an imported outline.
The bible's events go on the timeline too: drag them on from below, drag them along, and click one to open it or take it off.
Corkboard: click a card's title or synopsis to write it right on the card, its status word to change it, and its viewpoint line to choose a character.
Rows or Columns: in Columns each part is a column of its cards; drag a card to the foot of a column to move it into that part.
Small, medium or large cards (or Ctrl and the mouse wheel), and colour the cards by viewpoint, plot thread or status.

Plot threads: give a subplot, a relationship or a mystery a name, a colour and notes, tick it on the chapters and scenes it runs through, and see it as coloured tags on the corkboard cards. Choose one in the sidebar to show only its cards.
Filter the corkboard and timeline by viewpoint character.

Structure: five new shapes (four acts, story circle, Fichtean curve, mystery, romance) and your own, written as plain text; a beat can be carried by several chapters, and each beat keeps notes for the book.

Import planning: bring in a whole outline (parts, chapters and scenes with viewpoint, status, target, threads, beats and when), plot threads and structures from a text or Markdown file or from what you've copied. Export the plan the same way. The manual has a template for each.
Planning: double-click a corkboard card to write it.
Structure: the bar of the book names its chapters where there's room, and each beat's chapter is a drop-down box with the chapter's number and title instead of a heavy button.
Writing sprints: click the word count in the bar for a 10, 15, 25 or 45-minute sprint; the bar counts down and adds up the words you write across chapters, and a note says how it went.
Chapters and scenes with a word target show how far they've come with a thin line in the outline, gold once reached.
Fewer underlines: style hints start on Quiet (everyone is moved to it once; Full is a click away in Aa), are drawn thinner, and never show in the paragraph you're writing in.
Click the chapter's name in the writing bar for every part, chapter and scene with its words, and open one.
Line spacing in Aa: Close, Normal, Open or Double.
The saved note no longer flickers to Saving… while you type.

Places nest: the Places and Everything cards show only the outermost places, each with an "N inside ›" button into the places within it and a path back up. Finding still shows every place, and New place made while inside one goes in it.
Writing with no book chosen opens the book you last wrote in (or the one changed most recently) instead of asking you to pick one in the Library.
The paragraph style box in the writing bar is wide enough for its names.
An entry's page has an On this page row under its details, jumping to Family, In this place, Map, Gallery, Members, Relationships, Notes and Appears in.
Relationships are grouped by how they read (every Friend of together, A to Z), and a character's family is no longer listed a second time under Relationships.
Places can be shown as an outline: realms and places with the places inside them beneath, folding open and shut, each with its type and how many are inside.
Drag a place onto another place or a realm to put it inside; drag it onto the strip at the foot to take it out of everything.
The bible's website names each relative by what they are, as the PDF does: Father, Wife or Partner, Twin sister, Half-brother, Stepson, with names of one kind together.
The bible's PDF names each relative by what they are: Mother, Father, Wife or Husband (Partner when not married), Twin sister, Half-brother, Stepson, Adoptive mother, with names of one kind together.
Maps open over the whole page: zoom with the wheel about the pointer, drag to move about, drag pins to move them, and Fit to see it all.
Maps inside maps: a pinned place with its own map has a ring, its menu opens that map, and that map leads back up.
Pin names step aside rather than cover each other; pointing at a pin shows its name.
A place's page shows where it is (Elandroth › Aquiera › …) and what's in it: places inside, who lives or was born there, groups based there and what happened there; + Place inside makes one.
Creatures show the kinds they belong to the same way.

One tree per family however it's reached: a family found from two founders (a grandmother's sister, a wife) is no longer shown twice, and a founder's brothers and sisters are part of the founding generation.
People who joined a family are labelled by how: Married in, Partner, or Other parent.
Importing pages can replace all the text of entries already in the bible, keeping their pictures, gallery and map; an entry's page has Replace all its text with what you've copied.

The bible's website: a page for each kind (characters by gender or sex), a shorter home page with the first few of each, family kinds and a link to the family tree in each person's box, family trees at full size, the name first on phones and a menu that slides across.
In the bible's PDF, a family tree a little too tall for its page is made slightly smaller to stay with its heading.
Kinds of family: twins, half-, step-, adoptive and foster brothers and sisters, and adoptive, step and foster parents and children, in relationships, pasted pages and the family tree.
On the tree, adopted, step and foster lines are dotted and labelled, twins come down from one point, and someone with two partners sits between them.
Click a family member on a character's page to change what kind they are; the page names them (twin sister, stepfather, adopted son).
A founder with two partners no longer makes two copies of one family, and families sharing a surname are told apart (The Smith family (Hal's)).
Fourteen more typefaces come with Writing Studio: book serifs, a clean sans, handwriting, a typewriter, runes and display lettering, for books, covers, the bible and words set apart as you write.
Bible cards use the page's whole width, and summaries stop at two lines instead of running under the details.
Family trees are reworked: cards with a picture or initials, the name on up to two lines, a gender sign and an age, birth date or title.
Two parents of the same children who aren't partners are joined by a dashed line, and a key under the tree says what each line means.
The picked person sits in a bar above the tree with Parent, Partner, Child and Brother or sister buttons, and zoom sits in the board's corner.
Save as a picture… writes the tree you're looking at as a PNG, set for paper.
Share the bible as a PDF now carries a Family trees part, one tree to a page, turned when a tree is wider than tall; the bible's website gets a Family trees page.
Books on the shelf show where they stand: their status as a coloured tag, their word count, and a thin bar under the cover towards the book's word target.
The list view has a Words column and status tags, and shows the series with the book's number under it.
A world's and a series' pages give their totals under the title: how many books, how many words, and when one was last changed.
A book's panel opens with its words, chapters and when it was last changed at a glance, with progress towards its target when it has one.
Empty pictures in panels (a world's banner and logo, a series' cover) take a short box instead of a large empty one.
Find in the bible: a box at the top of Worldbuilding narrows the cards as you type, matching names, other names, summaries and details.

Bible cards show more at a glance: a smaller picture, the kind and its race or type, two lines of summary, and a few details as chips (Age 54, Eyes grey). Gender signs are drawn, so they show on every computer.

The side panel on the cards is now a summary of the world: how many entries of each kind (click one to see them), what changed lately, and quick actions: a new entry, importing many pages, copying a blank page, sharing the bible.
The sidebar is in two clear parts, Entries and The world, with kinds that have nothing yet shown more quietly.
Check these kinds is now a one-line note you can open, rather than a box at the top of every page.

Choices in side panels (kind, gender, race and the rest, everywhere in the Studio) are framed like the text boxes with the value on the left. The paste tools moved to the foot of an entry's panel, under Pages from elsewhere.

A new writing bar, laid out like a word processor's: groups for Style, Font, Paragraph, Insert, Review, Edit and View, each named beneath, with clear drawn icons, and each tool's name and shortcut when you point at it. A Link button joins them.
A typeface box like Word's: it shows the selection's font by name, and its list has the book's typeface and this world's fonts, each in its own lettering, with Add fonts to this world.
The chapter's name sits between the previous and next arrows, beside the hints and the word count and whether it's saved.
On a narrow window, the less-used groups fold into More, which names every tool with its shortcut, so nothing is cut off any more.

Set words in your world's fonts as you write: select runes, symbols, a character's handwriting or a letter, and choose a typeface from the new Ff button on the editor's toolbar. The words show in that font in Writing, on the typeset pages and PDFs, and in the ebook and its preview (inside the EPUB when the font's licence allows).
Words in a world font aren't spell-checked or given style hints, since they're not English.
If a font is removed from the world, its words go back to the book's own typeface, and Typesetting says so.

Your own fonts, per world: Worldbuilding › Fonts imports TrueType font files, puts a family's regular, italic, bold and bold italic together, and shows each in a line of its own type. Every book in the world can then use them for its pages and PDFs, its cover and its ebook, and Share the bible can use them for the website and the bible's PDF. They're kept in the library folder, so they go wherever the library goes.
Fonts that can't be printed properly are turned away with the reason: PostScript-outline (CFF) .otf files, web fonts, font collections, and fonts whose licence forbids putting them in documents.
Typesetting's typeface is now a list, so any number of typefaces fit.

Import many pages: a whole bible, or a good part of one, from a text, Markdown, Word or OpenDocument file or from what you've copied (Ctrl+V on the cards does it too). Pages start at their Name: lines or title headings; headings such as “# Characters” or a “Kind: Place” line say what kind they are. Each page fills the entry of its name or a new one, pages that name each other link up, a backup is made first, and Ctrl+Z takes the whole import back.
The user manual has a blank page for every kind of entry, ready to fill in and paste or import.
Lore's “Details” section, written under its own heading in a pasted page, now goes to that section instead of the detail lines.

Family trees keep families apart: each family starts from its own founders, and someone who married in appears on the tree marked “Married in”, with a link to their own family, instead of pulling their parents and cousins in.

Two views: a family's whole tree from its founders down (from the Family trees list), and one person's own tree (their lines up, brothers and sisters, partners and descendants). Each has a link to the other.

Smoother to use: click someone to pick them (their lines light up, and the panel shows their parents, partners, brothers and sisters and children), double-click to see the tree from them, add a parent, partner, child or brother or sister from the toolbar, and zoom with −, Fit and + or the keyboard (arrows look around, + and − zoom, 0 fits, Esc goes back). Zooming and moving glide.

Pasted relationships fill in properly: a fuller form of a name finds the entry (“Yonvaan Akumes Yerasuun” finds Yonvaan Yerasuun), “The” doesn't matter, and wordings like Grandparents, Former teacher, Crew of and Taught by are understood.

What a pasted page names that the bible doesn't have is made: a person, place or group in Family or Relationships becomes a new entry of the right kind, linked; a race or realm in the details joins the bible's Races or Realms. Undo the paste takes them away again.
Copy a blank page to fill in: a template for the entry's kind, with your world's sections and books. Lines left blank are ignored when it's pasted back.

Your own kinds of relationship: any wording in a pasted page's Relationships that Writing Studio doesn't know (Admires, Haunted by) becomes one of your world's relationships and is linked, reading the other way from the other side (Admired by, Haunts). Worldbuilding › Relationships lists them with their links, makes new ones, renames them (their links follow) and changes how they read from the other side; Add a relationship offers them.

A whole page pasted onto an entry now replaces what was there, part by part: the name, other names, how it's said, the summary, the details, each section and book's notes it has, the notes, and the relationships of each kind it lists. Parts it doesn't have are left alone, and Undo the paste (Ctrl+Z) still puts everything back, links included.

Reset the bible, at the foot of the Worldbuilding sidebar: move every entry to the Trash, or start completely afresh (languages, image boards, page templates and choices too). A backup is made first and Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Share the bible is now a page in Worldbuilding where you choose everything first: a website or a PDF, for you or as a reader's guide, what goes in (pictures and maps, family and relationships, the glossary, languages), and for a website its theme (Parchment, Clean, Night sky, Grimoire, Atlas), light or dark, colour, typefaces, title and tagline, cards or lists, search and kind colours, with a sketch of the look as you choose. The choices are kept with the world.

The bible website is redesigned: a home page with the title over your banner and picture cards for every entry, entry pages with a side box of picture, details, family and relationships, previous and next links, search on every page, a glossary with letters to jump to, and pages that fit phones.
Your languages are in the shared bible: a Languages page on the website with a dictionary for each and a box to find a word, and a Languages part in the PDF.
Seven more cover layouts: Arch, Medallion, Sidebar, Stacked, Starfield, Ornate and Modern.
Writing Studio opens on Your worlds: a card for each world with its banner, description, counts and covers, and one for books outside any world.
Race, realm and type of place offer only what you've made or written, with New race, New realm or plane and Write a new one at the foot of their menus.

Paste a whole bible page: copy a character sheet (Name, Other names, How it's said, Summary, Details, sections like Appearance or History, Notes per book, Family, Relationships, Spoilers) and paste it onto an entry, or press Ctrl+V on the bible's cards to make a new entry from it. Each part goes to its place: sections into the page's own (Appearance into “Appearance & personality”), notes to each book by title or “Book 2”, and family and relationships become links to entries already in the bible. Ctrl+Z or “Undo the paste” puts it back.

Sections can be choices: in a kind's sections, “Status: Alive | Dead | Missing” shows those as buttons to pick from, with a box to write something else instead; “Traits (any): Brave | Loyal | Proud” lets you pick several.

Pasting into chapters: text from Google Docs no longer turns all bold, and its bold and italics are kept; Word's hidden formatting goes; quotes turn curly, “--” becomes a dash and “...” an ellipsis, as when typing; blank paragraphs and typed indents go; “***” lines become scene breaks; plain text joins lines wrapped short. Pictures can be pasted straight into the text.
The side panel's boxes tidy what's pasted: several lines pasted into a one-line box (a name, other names) are joined rather than cut off.
Your world's own languages: Worldbuilding › Languages. Each language is a list of words with their meaning, part of speech, how they're said and notes, edited on the page and in the side panel.

Import a language from a spreadsheet (CSV or TSV), an SFM lexicon (Toolbox, Lexique Pro, FieldWorks), a plain word list (“khaz = mountain”) or a NorthRay .nrlang file; into a new language or added to one you have. Export as .nrlang or CSV.

The spell checker knows them: a word from one of your languages isn't marked as a misspelling, words built from its endings and beginnings (“-in”, “ve-”) count too, and a near miss is marked with the right word suggested: “Did you mean the Telvani word ‘veyth’ar’ (light)?”
Ctrl+K takes you anywhere: type a few letters of a chapter, scene, bible entry or book and press Enter. Ctrl+/ shows every keyboard shortcut. (Link in the text is now Ctrl+Alt+K.)
A smooth typing cursor that glides to where you type, and a clearer save note: “Saved just now”, “Saved a moment ago”, “Saved 5 minutes ago”.
Each chapter remembers where you'd scrolled to, and Undo now works after closing and reopening a book, stepping back through earlier versions of the chapter.
Warm night paper for writing in the dark: choose it under Aa.
Style hints wait until you pause typing before they appear.
A thin bar under the top bar fills with today's words against your daily goal.
Planning cards and timeline lanes are coloured by their viewpoint character, and Planning opens long books faster.
The family tree zooms with Ctrl + mouse wheel and moves when you drag its background. Bible cards have bigger portraits.
Clicking a comment in Review brings its words to the middle of the page and lights them up for a moment.
A clearer line shows where a chapter or scene will land when you drag it in the outline, and the text's right-click menu has fewer, clearer items.
NorthRay Capture can show the word count of the chapter you're writing, including what you've just typed.

NorthRay Capture now follows your writing as it happens: the chapter you're on, today's words (counting what you've just typed, before it's saved) and the book's word count are shared within two seconds, instead of every 30 seconds, through the same small file on this PC.
The book you're writing (its title, series line and cover) is shared with NorthRay Capture's book card, through the same small file on this PC that shares today's words with NorthRay Launcher.
A writing streak now counts every day you write anything, whether or not you reach your daily goal.
Today's words, your goal and your streak are shared with NorthRay Launcher's home page (a small file on this PC only).

Fixed: clicking OK (or any button) in a question box did nothing when Windows' display scaling was above 100%; only Enter worked. The box was drawn smaller than the places it took clicks. This is what stopped Review › Names › “Change to” from working with the mouse.

Fixed: “Change to” now changes every use of the name, including ones in curly quotes (“Marren, wait!”), with a possessive (Marren’s), or next to a dash or an ellipsis. Before, those were skipped. “Appears in” counts them too.

Choosing who a relationship is with (and a parent, partner, brother or sister, or child) now has a search field: type part of a name and the list narrows. Long lists scroll with the mouse wheel or Page Up and Page Down, so every entry can be reached.
Any long pop-up list in Writing Studio works the same way.

Right-click a name in Writing: “Add “Maren” to the bible…” (as whichever kind), or “Open “Maren” in the bible” when it's there. A name of several words (“Maren Holt”) is taken whole, or select the words you want.
New names as you write: Writing's panel lists names in the open chapter that aren't in the bible yet, with “Add to the bible…” and “Not a name”.

Maps: a place's or realm's page can have a map, any picture you've made. “+ Pin an entry…” and a click on the map puts it there; click a pin to open it, move it or take it off. Places lists your maps.

Checks (Worldbuilding's sidebar): names spelt like a bible name, facts that disagree (two lines of an entry's details, or its eyes, hair or age against what the text says about them), and entries never named in the text. Anything can be marked as fine.
Glossary (Worldbuilding's sidebar): every name and other name from A to Z, with how it's said (“How it's said” on each page) and its line or two.
Magic and powers: a kind of its own, with pages for how it works, its rules, costs and limits, who can use it and what it can't do.
Spoilers: mark any fact (a detail, a section, the summary, or the whole entry) as revealed in a later book. The page shows it, and a reader's guide leaves it out for readers of earlier books.

Share the bible: a website (a folder of linked pages, with the glossary, families, relationships, maps and galleries, ready to put online), or a printable bible as a PDF, typeset like a book. Either can be everything, or a reader's guide up to the end of a chosen book, without spoilers from later books or your notes.

Family trees: a character's page has a Family section with their parents, partners, brothers and sisters, and children (anyone sharing a parent counts as a brother or sister), with “+ Parent”, “+ Partner”, “+ Brother or sister” and “+ Child”: someone already in the bible, or a new character opened with its name ready to type.

“See the family tree”: the whole family drawn by generation, partners side by side (two lines for a marriage), lines down to their children. Click anyone to open their page. A wide tree shrinks to fit; wider still, Shift and the mouse wheel move across it.
Characters lists the bible's families (“The Wren family · 7”), each opening its tree. Families are named after the surname most of them share.
A character's Race lists only your own races: the bible's Races and the races you've written on characters. There's no built-in list of elves, dwarves and so on any more.
“New race…” in the Race list makes a race in the bible and opens it with its name ready to type.

Entry pages in the world bible: each kind has its sections (a character: Appearance & personality, Backstory & goals, Abilities & powers, Age, birth & status). Written sections show on the page in full; the rest wait under “Still to write” — click one to write it in the panel.
Change the sections every page of a kind has (“Change the sections every Character page has…”): one per line, for the whole world. Writing already in a section you take out stays on the page.
Notes per book: what happens to an entry in each book, written for one book at a time and shown on its page under the book's name.
A gallery in every entry: add pictures of it (art, sketches, references), caption them, and choose which is the main picture.
Image boards inside entries: “+ New board” on an entry's page makes a board kept there, not in the sidebar. A board from the sidebar can be moved onto an entry's page from its panel (“Kept in”).
Merging two copies of an entry keeps both sets of sections, pictures and book notes.

The world bible tidies itself: copies of one entry (the same name, either apostrophe) are merged into one, keeping every name, detail, picture and relationship. The merged copies go to the Trash, so one can be brought back. A character and a creature of the same name become one character that is that creature.
When a book joins a world, its own bible entries move into the world's bible (merging any it already has).
Fixed: “Add to the bible” in Review › Names could add the same name again and again.

“Check these kinds”: entries that look filed under the wrong kind are pointed out (Zornov's race is Demon, so Demon reads like a race), with “Make it a Race” or “Keep it”. Right-click any entry's card to change its kind.

Creatures, one level at a time: each species as a card; click it for its kinds; click a kind for the named characters of that kind. A path back up at the top, “+ Add a kind”, and drag a card onto another to move it under it. A character can be a creature too (“A creature?” on its page).
Bigger gender and sex signs on character cards and group headings.

The cover designer works for every edition. For a paperback, hardback or large print edition it makes the whole print cover (back, spine and front) at that edition's trim size and spine width, with 0.125 in bleed, as a print-ready PDF at 300 pixels per inch.

The back cover carries your blurb (it starts as the book's synopsis) and keeps a white space for the ISBN barcode the printer adds; the spine has the title and author once it's wide enough for words (0.25 in).
Easier to find: “Design a cover…” under the cover in a book's details, “Design the print cover…” in Spine and cover, and a link in Publishing's sidebar for whichever edition is open.
“Use the front as the ebook cover” makes the matching 1600 × 2560 ebook cover from the same design.

Design a cover: Publishing › Cover and look › “Design a cover…” makes an ebook cover from the title, author and series line, at 1600 × 2560 pixels (the size ebook stores ask for). Four layouts (Classic frame, Picture, Picture and band, Minimal), seven colour sets, your own picture if you like, and the typeface. The design is kept, so the cover can be changed later.

EPUBs look like the printed book: chapters open as in your Typesetting design (“Chapter One” over the title, or a large number), with the drop cap and first words in small capitals if you chose them, your own scene-break symbol, and left-aligned text if you set that. Prologues and front matter are never numbered.
The book's typeface goes inside the ebook (with its licence), and the copyright page says what it's set in. Readers can still choose their own.
A choice of spaced paragraphs with no indent, for non-fiction ebooks.
The cover fills the screen on every e-reader, whatever its shape.
“Read it as an ebook” shows the same styling as the EPUB.

Review copies for beta readers: Review › Comments › “Make a review copy…” saves the book as one web page. Your reader opens it in any browser, selects words to comment on them (or comments on a whole chapter), and sends you back the small file it makes. “Import a reader’s comments…” puts each comment on the words it was about, with the reader’s name.
Messages and questions (“Delete this?”, “Saved”) now appear in a NorthRay dialog that matches the app, instead of the plain grey Windows box.
Clearer top bar: the tabs you're not on are brighter against the night sky.
Words and names with apostrophes (Zah’mes, Brennick’s) can be added to the dictionary and match the bible, whichever apostrophe you type (’ or ').
Ctrl+Backspace and Ctrl+Delete remove a whole word at a time.
Page width has a new “Fit” setting: the text fills the window.
Long words move whole to the next line; the editor never breaks a word with a hyphen.
Fixed: Enter in a bulleted or numbered list didn't start a new item.
Text on the night sky stays clear: stars keep away from the words in title bars and sidebars.

Fancy dialogue tags are marked far less: an action as a tag only when a comma joins it to the speech (“Fine,” she smiled), never after a question, an exclamation or a full stop (“What’s the matter, Blue?” I sighed / “We need this.” I laughed).
Groups and races have Members: the people (and creatures) in them as cards, "+ Add members…" to tick them in and out, and a cross to take one out.

Characters can be grouped by gender or sex, by race, or not at all (Group by, at the top of Characters). Creatures are split by their top-level kind (Dragon: the dragon, its types and the dragons themselves).
Fixed: the fix buttons on style hints ("Change to…", "Remove…", rewrites) didn't change anything. They all work now.

Fancy dialogue tags and tag adverbs are only marked on real tags, verbs attached to the speech (“Go,” he hissed / She hissed, “Go.”), not actions after it (“Then I just-” Bluebolt roared; “Fine.” I laughed warmly). And only when it's overdone: an action as a tag (she smiled), the same tag a third time, or six or more and over twice the plain ones.
"seemed to know" is offered as "knew" instead of being cut.

Creatures are a family tree of your own: each can be "A kind of" another creature in the bible (Dragon › Glimmerwyrm › Bluebolt). They nest that way in Worldbuilding, and your top-level kinds are filters in the sidebar. The fixed list of creature types is gone.

The Writing Studio now has the NorthRay look, like the Launcher, Browser and Files: a new icon (an open book under the aurora and the north star), the night sky and aurora along the top with the NorthRay mark, and NorthRay's cool colours with aurora green in the app and the writing page, in light and dark. Everything works as before.

Comic scripts: set a book's Format to "Comic script" (its details panel). Writing then has Page, Panel, Dialogue, Caption and SFX (style menu, or Alt+1 to Alt+5); typing "PAGE ", "PANEL ", "CAPTION: ", "SFX: " or a name and a colon ("TOM: ") starts that kind of line, and Enter moves on to the likely next one. Pages, panels and balloons are numbered for you as you write: PAGE ONE (right · two panels), Panel 1, 1. CAPTION:, 2. TOM:.

The "Comic script" typesetting design sets the script the way artists and letterers expect: Courier Prime on US Letter, each comic page on a new page, panels and balloons numbered, names in bold capitals. Export it from Typesetting as a PDF.
The world bible is grouped by the book each entry first appears in, in series reading order ("Not in a book yet" last). Places inside other places sit with them, marked "in …".
Characters are split by gender or sex within each book, with a sign on each card.
Races and Realms are categories in the bible. A character's race and realm (and a place's or creature's realm) are chosen from the bible's own; choosing a common one it doesn't have yet adds it.
The small text links are now proper buttons.

Every kind of style hint now explains itself and suggests a fix: break a long sentence at a natural point, start a "There was" sentence with its subject, rewrite "was eaten by the dog" as "the dog ate", join repeated sentence starts, swap "said quietly" for "whispered", and filter words come with an example of showing instead.
Fancy dialogue tags are only marked when it's overdone: tags that are actions ("she smiled"), more fancy tags than plain ones, or the same one again and again.
Spelling suggestions catch jumbled letters ("Capitan" → "Captain") and words written as one ("alot" → "a lot").

Worldbuilding: a new Creatures kind; characters can be filtered by gender or sex, race, and realm; places by type and realm; creatures by type. Choose them in the details panel; what you've already written as "Gender:" or "Race:" lines counts.
Each kind of entry has its own colour, on the Worldbuilding cards, in the name links in your text and on the name cards.
Relationships suit the kind of entry: a place offers "Located in", "Borders", "Capital of" and "Home of" rather than family ties, and the entries that fit come first.

Review › Names: "Change to …" corrects a name everywhere in the book (the old text stays in each chapter's versions); "Add to the bible" asks what kind of entry it is. Names with curly apostrophes (Zah’mes) now match the bible, and word forms (Fluxian, Elven) aren't taken for misspellings.
"Show it" and Appears in open the chapter with the name highlighted and scrolled into view.
Front matter and back matter: a chapter-level section can be marked as either (Kind in its details). They're never numbered, so Chapter 1 stays Chapter 1, and front matter keeps roman page numbers.
Typesetting keeps the symbols you use for point of view (✧, 🗡, 🪶, ★): characters the book font doesn't have come from bundled symbol fonts (Noto, OFL) instead of empty boxes.
Hide the outline or the details panel for more room: the two buttons beside Settings, or F3 and F4.
Links look cleaner: no underlines, a soft highlight when you point at them.

Style hints offer fixes you can click: remove a doubled word, a filler word or a dialogue-tag adverb; change a fancy tag to "said" or "asked"; plainer phrasings for clichés ("in the nick of time" → "just in time"); "began to run" → "ran"; the spelling or dash the chapter mostly uses; and your own rules' replacements.
Echoes suggest other words and phrases to use instead, and can show you the earlier use.

A thesaurus: select a word or a phrase (or put the cursor in a word) and press ≈ on the toolbar or Ctrl+Shift+O for other ways to say it, in the same form ("passed away" → "died", "kicked the bucket"). Built from WordNet, works offline.
Spelling suggestions reach words that are several letters off ("skelingtons" suggests "skeletons", "definately" suggests "definitely"), not just one-letter slips.

Long names skip middle names too: "Albus Percival Wulfric Brian Dumbledore" links as Albus Dumbledore, Albus Brian Dumbledore and so on, as long as the first or last name is there. A middle name on its own still doesn't link.

Characters' names link by their first or last name on their own, or by runs that include one of them: for "Snarf Jill Grave", Snarf, Grave, Snarf Grave, Snarf Jill and Jill Grave all link, but Jill alone doesn't (a middle name is rarely used by itself). Names written in capitals ("JACKSON!") are found too.

A spell checker of the Studio's own, with British or American English dictionaries to match the book's language. It knows every name in your bible, accepts Oxford -ize spellings in British English, and keeps a dictionary for each world (or independent book). Hover a mistake for suggestions (click one to use it), Add to the dictionary, or Ignore once. Your added words are listed with your style rules.
Fixed: style hints could stay switched off after updating. They're now on (Full) unless you chose Off.

Worldbuilding pages link to each other like a wiki: names of other entries in a summary, details or notes are links (a name shared by several offers a choice), and each page lists the entries that mention it under Linked from.

Image boards: boards of pictures for a world or an independent book (characters, maps, places, moods). Drag pictures anywhere, resize them by the corner, caption them, tie them to an entry (and use one as the entry's picture). Pictures are kept in the library and listed in Artwork.

Planning has three views. Corkboard: your chapters and scenes as index cards pinned to a cork board (the pin is the status). Drag a card beside another to move it before or after, or onto the middle of a chapter to make a scene part of it.

Timeline: place chapters and scenes on the story's own calendar (days, weeks, months or years, plus words such as "Midsummer, 1204"), in a lane for each viewpoint character. Drag a card along to move it in time. A line joins them in reading order and turns orange where the story jumps back, so flashbacks stand out.

Structure: lay a story shape over the book (three acts, fifteen beats, the hero's journey, seven points, five acts or kishōtenketsu). The book is shown by length with each beat marked, each beat says which chapter falls there, and you can match beats to chapters and see whether yours come early or late. An empty book can be outlined from a structure in one step.

Characters' names link by their parts too: "Maren Ada Holt" is also found as Maren, Holt or Maren Holt (titles and words such as "of" don't count on their own). When characters share a name, it links to all of them and its card shows each one. Worldbuilding's "Appears in" and the cards' cast use the same rule, and a full name is no longer counted twice.
Fixed: choosing from a menu opened by a button could act on the wrong item, or close the Studio.
Every pop-up menu (right-click menus, and choices such as an entry's kind or a chapter's status) now has the NorthRay look, in light or dark, instead of the plain Windows menu.
Hover a name from your Worldbuilding bible in the text to see its card: picture (or initials), name, kind, other names, summary and the first few details, with Open in Worldbuilding.

Style hints, rebuilt: they now tell dialogue from narration, so characters can talk naturally. New kinds: echoes (the same word again within a few lines), repeated sentence starts, adverbs on dialogue tags, fancy dialogue tags, redundancies ("nodded his head"), clichés, and mixed spellings or dash styles. Names from your bible are never counted as echoes.

Hints have three modes: Off, Quiet (only clear slips, the new default) and Full. Click the hint count in the editor's toolbar to turn each kind on or off, see how many are in the chapter, jump from one to the next, and see a reading-ease figure.
Hover a hint to see why it's marked, with Ignore once, Ignore it everywhere in this world, or Turn off this kind.

Your own style rules, kept with the world (or with the book when it isn't in a world): flag words, suggest a replacement, limit how often a word is used, flag a word used again too soon, keep to one spelling of a name, or, for experts, a pattern (run safely, so it can never freeze the editor). Each shows how many times it matches in the open chapter as you make it. Rules can be exported and imported as files to share.
No more status bar along the bottom of the window. Messages appear for a moment as a small note near the bottom instead. Today's words are at the foot of the outline while you write.
A Writing view panel (Aa in the editor's toolbar): Serif, Book, Sans or Typewriter type, four sizes, and a narrow, normal or wide page. Your choices are remembered.
Focus mode (Ctrl+Shift+F): the outline and details panel step aside, and everything but the paragraph you're in fades back.
Typewriter scrolling (Ctrl+Shift+T): the line you're typing stays near the middle of the window.
Spell check can be turned off and on (it uses Windows' own dictionaries; right-click a word for suggestions).
Style hints (off until you turn them on): doubled words, filler words, maybe-passive verbs and long sentences get a gentle underline. Hover one to see why. They never change your text.
Names from your Worldbuilding bible are linked in the text: Ctrl+click one to open its page.

Backups: a copy every 30 minutes while you work (when something changed) and when you close the Studio, as well as when the library opens. In Settings you can have them copied to a second folder too, such as another drive or a synced folder.

Minimise, maximise and close are now part of the app's own top area, like NorthRay Browser, instead of a separate Windows title bar. Drag the empty part of the top to move the window; double-click it to maximise. On Windows 11, pointing at maximise shows the snap layouts.
Maintenance release.
Maintenance release.

Comments: select some words and choose Comment (✎) in the toolbar, or press Ctrl+Alt+M, to leave a note on them. A chapter's details list its comments, and Review has a Comments section for the whole book.
Resolve a comment once it's dealt with: it stays with its words, unhighlighted, and can be reopened. Comments never appear in the PDF or EPUB.
The "preview" notes are gone from the About box, Settings, Typesetting and Publishing, which now say what the Studio includes.
Maintenance release, with screenshots of the Studio in NorthRay Launcher and on the website.
Settings are read more carefully: a setting saved by another version can no longer stop the Studio starting.
Maintenance release.

Review (new): compare any chapter or scene with an earlier version or a snapshot. Added words are shaded and removed words struck through, with counts, and you can restore the older text (the current one is kept, so it can be undone).
Snapshots: save the whole book as it is (before a revision, before sending it to an editor) and see later which chapters changed and by how much. Snapshots are kept until you remove them.

Names: a continuity check finds spellings close to a name in the world's bible (“Marren” for “Maren”) and names used often that aren't in it yet. Add one as another name, add it to the bible, or mark it as fine.
Goals: set a daily word goal and see today's words, the last 7 and 28 days, your streak, and a chart of each day. Writing's status bar shows today's progress.
Libraries are upgraded automatically.

Planning (new): the Planning tab shows every chapter and scene as a card on a board, in the order of the book and grouped by part. Each card shows its status (with a coloured edge), synopsis, viewpoint character, and words against its target.
Cards show which characters appear in each chapter and scene, found in the text from the world's bible.
Word targets for the book and for each chapter or scene, with progress in the sidebar and on the cards. Filter the board by status: outline, draft, revised or final.
Choose a chapter's or scene's viewpoint character from the world's characters. The panel lists every entry that appears in it, linked to Worldbuilding.
Move cards earlier or later, add chapters and scenes, and open any of them in Writing. Libraries are upgraded automatically.
Worldbuilding (new): every world keeps a bible of characters, places, groups, things, lore and events, shared by all its books. Independent books get their own.
Each entry has other names it goes by, a summary, a picture, a list of details (Age: 34, Eyes: grey), and notes.
Relationships between entries read correctly from both sides: “Lives in Highcliff” on a character shows as “Home of” on the place.
Appears in: each entry lists the chapters and scenes its name (or another name it goes by) appears in, with how often and the first time in context. Click one to open it in Writing.
A world's page in the Library summarises its entries. Entries go to the Trash and can be restored.

Editions (new): each book can have a paperback, hardback, large-print and ebook edition, each with its own ISBN. Print editions can have their own trim size and design; a new large-print edition starts with the large-print design.
Publishing works one edition at a time: print editions get their checks, spine and cover measurements, a print-ready PDF and a proof; the ebook edition gets the EPUB.
The copyright page, in print and in the EPUB, lists every edition's ISBN.
Checks fit the edition: no print checks for the ebook, no ebook cover check for print, and a warning if two editions share an ISBN.
Existing books get a paperback (with the book's ISBN and its publishing settings) and an ebook edition the first time Publishing opens them. Libraries are upgraded automatically.
Publishing (new): the Publishing tab checks the book, gives the measurements for its cover, and makes the files for printers and ebook stores.

Print-ready PDF in the PDF/X-1a format print-on-demand printers ask for: text in pure black, pictures in grey (or CMYK for a colour interior), fonts embedded, and an optional 0.125-inch bleed on the outside edges.

EPUB 3 ebook export, with an EPUB 2 contents file for older readers: cover, title and copyright pages, a contents list with parts and chapters, pictures cropped and sized for e-readers, and accessibility information. It uses the same chapters as the Preview.
Pre-flight checks: missing author, description or cover; an ISBN with a wrong check digit; pictures without a description, or that would print blurred; too few pages for a paperback.
Spine width for white or cream paper, and the full cover size with bleed, for your cover designer. Check them against your printer's own cover template before the cover is finished.

Preview (new): see the book as an ebook on a phone, a 6-inch e-ink reader or a tablet. Turn pages by clicking or with the arrow keys, and try the reader's own settings: white, sepia or night pages, text size, and the book's typeface, a serif or a sans-serif.
Typesetting: zoom (fit, actual size, 200%), single pages as well as spreads, and guides showing the margins, the baseline grid and the spine edge.
Typesetting: chapter openings with “Chapter One” above the title, or a large numeral; drop caps; front matter numbered i, ii, iii, with the story starting at page 1 on a right-hand page.
Chapters already titled “Chapter 3: …” keep their number; prologues, acknowledgements and the like aren't numbered.
Typesetting: a contents page with page numbers (parts in small capitals, chapters indented).
Typesetting: a copyright page on the back of the title page, made only from the book's own details (author, edition, ISBN); with none of those it stays blank.
Typesetting: chapters can open with their first words in small capitals.
Typesetting: margin controls (inside, outside, top and bottom).
Exported PDFs are much smaller: only the letters used are embedded.
PDF import: a title page in large type stays front matter instead of becoming chapters; “CHAPTER ONE” joins the title on the line below it; placeholder details such as “unspecified” are ignored.
Typesetting (new): the Typesetting tab sets your whole book as printed pages and shows them as two-page spreads. Text is justified and hyphenated, with real kerning, ligatures and small capitals.
Paragraphs are set as a whole (the Knuth–Plass method TeX uses), so spacing stays even. Widows and orphans are prevented, and chapters open part-way down a new page.
Pages include a title page, part pages, running heads (book title on the left, chapter on the right), page numbers, scene breaks, and your pictures with their crops and captions.

Four starting designs (Classic, Open, Ragged right, Large print), plus typeface, type size, line spacing, trim size, justified or ragged text, hyphenation, chapters on right-hand pages, running heads and title page. Each book remembers its design.
Export the typeset book as a PDF with the fonts embedded and text that can be searched and copied. Print-ready PDF/X for printers comes with publishing.
Bundled book fonts: Crimson Text and Gentium Book (SIL Open Font License). British and US English hyphenation.

Artwork library: a new Artwork page lists every picture in your library, stored once however many chapters use it. Add pictures, name them, mark them as a map, illustration, ornament and so on, and see which chapters use each one.
Pictures in the text can be cropped, sized and aligned from the details panel: drag the frame or its corners to crop. The stored picture is never changed, so a crop can always be undone.
Print checks: each picture shows its printed size and resolution for the book's trim size, with a warning below 300 ppi and a stronger one below 150, and a one-click size that prints sharply.
Books have a trim size (6 × 9 in, A5, B-format and more), and measurements can be shown in inches, centimetres, millimetres or pixels (Settings).
New pictures start at the widest size that prints sharply. Pictures that came with imported books are listed in the artwork library too.
+ Scene now adds a *** divider at the end of the chapter, with the cursor ready for the new scene, instead of a separate page.
Captions and screen-reader descriptions for pictures.

No more Windows menu bar: every command has a place in the window. A new Settings page (in the top bar, or Ctrl+,) holds the library folder, export and backup, the theme and a full list of keyboard shortcuts; New book and Import sit on the Library page; Move to Trash is in the details panel; the editor toolbar has previous and next chapter buttons.
Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down move to the previous or next chapter, from the text or the outline.
Saving... then Saved, in the editor and the status bar, so you can see your words are stored.
The Studio reopens the book and chapter you were working on.
Double-click a book to open it in Writing. New chapters, scenes and parts start with their title selected; press Enter to go straight to the text.
An empty chapter shows a faint prompt; a new library offers Create a book and Import a book.
One details panel layout for books, chapters and scenes, in tidy sections; the outline lines up with the Library sidebar.
The import preview fits the window, and switching chapters no longer flickers.
No scroll bars anywhere, including the longer text boxes; the wheel and keys still scroll.

Word (.docx) and OpenDocument (.odt) import: chapters from heading styles (or from lines like "CHAPTER ONE" when there are none), parts, italic, bold, small caps, quotes, lists, pictures, links, footnotes (gathered into Notes) and the document's title and author. Tracked changes come in as accepted.
Fixed: some documents' formatting was ignored when it was set through their styles.
Smoother animations: eased page changes, status messages that fade in and out, and softer hover effects.
Book covers lift slightly on hover; the workspace tabs, sidebar and outline highlights slide to your choice; the import tick boxes animate.
The Bookshelf/List switch no longer overlaps the filter button.
Fixes the Studio closing while importing: files are now read by a separate helper process, so a file the importer can't handle shows an explanation instead of closing the app.
Unexpected errors while reading or importing are explained rather than closing the app.
If the Studio ever does close unexpectedly, it notes where in crash.log (in %LOCALAPPDATA%\NorthRay\Writing Studio) so the cause can be found.
The Writing workspace: parts, chapters and scenes in an outline you can drag to rearrange, with word counts and a status for each.

A page-like editor with paragraph styles (Body, First paragraph, Centred, Epigraph, Attribution, Verse, Letter, Note, headings), bold, italic, underline, small caps, scene breaks, quotes, lists and pictures.
Saves as you type; keeps an earlier version of each chapter and scene every ten minutes or so (the last 40), which you can restore.

Import from EPUB (parts, chapters, front and back matter, styling, pictures, title, author and cover), HTML, Markdown and plain text, with a preview to choose what comes in. DRM-protected books are refused.
PDF import (experimental): chapters and paragraphs are worked out from the page layout, so check the result.
Subtle animations throughout, and hidden scroll bars.
First preview (Milestone 1): the Author Library.
Worlds, series and books, including standalone books and books outside any world.
Separate reading and chronological order for every series; drag and drop to reorder or move.
Covers, world banners and logos; details edited in a side panel that saves as you type.
A safe local library: every change saved at once, a backup each time it opens, the Trash, and JSON export.
